acceptance.predicate: the mechanism used to pass the timeout is quoted from model_access.py with file:line
acceptance.evidence: guarded_create(client, *, lane, **kwargs) at model_access.py:584 forwards **kwargs verbatim to `response = client.messages.create(**kwargs)` at model_access.py:600. Passing timeout=tier2_timeout/tier3_timeout into guarded_create therefore reaches the Anthropic SDK as a per-request timeout, overriding the client-level http timeout=60.0 set at model_access.py:650. Wall-clock enforcement (the .result(timeout=) future) is what guarantees return even against a client that ignores the kwarg; the kwarg bounds the real SDK call so the abandoned worker unwinds at the same deadline.

findings.claim: Two LLM call sites exist in router.py (tier2 at the router-standard lane, tier3 at the router-deep lane); both are now timeout-bounded. Grep of router.py shows no guarded_create/messages.create call left without a paired .result(timeout=).

Design choice: a tier2 timeout returns a well-formed failure immediately rather than falling through to tier3, so a slow standard tier cannot stack tier2_timeout + tier3_timeout (5s + 15s) of latency onto one turn. The note permits either fall-through or a well-formed failure; the failure was chosen for latency.

LLM calls run on a dedicated _llm_pool (max_workers=4), not the 2-worker _tier_pool that every route() opens with for T0+knowledge concurrency, so a timed-out model call cannot starve that concurrency. An abandoned worker is bounded by the timeout= kwarg forwarded to the real SDK (model_access.py:600); a client that ignores its own deadline keeps a worker only until it self-completes.

The handler runs route() off the caller thread. Verified SAFE here because _handle_route_chat wires no command_fn into the TieredRouter (so route() executes no SynapseCommands and touches no hou.* API). A guarding comment records the invariant: if a hou-touching command_fn is ever wired here, the offload must be revisited.

Runtime is Python 3.14.2 on this host (CLAUDE.md header says 3.13). concurrent.futures.TimeoutError is the builtin TimeoutError on 3.11+, so the _FutureTimeout alias catches both; no version-specific behaviour.
